doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Borrowed horns in Detroit
summary: Foster clarifies that after his instruments were stolen he borrowed saxophones, one from Al Cafagna.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I may have mislead you earlier when I said something about not having instruments. I played on borrowed instruments in Detroit after having had mine stolen. I was able to borrow an instrument almost immediately to play.
People must like you, because a saxophone is not something that you generally -- it’s very personal. It’s like your tongue. It’s like an extension of your mouth. Can I borrow your tongue?
I don’t think. So you must have had some good esteem with people. People must have liked you.
I suppose they respected my playing ability.
Which one did you borrow? Just curious.
There was a guy named Al Cafagna [correct]. He wasn’t well known. He was a musician. He owned a tenor saxophone. He wasn’t that good a player. He thought, “I might as well let this guy use it.”
Somebody use it that could do something with it [laughs].
